model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Nim (4 piles) with action format 'pile,take'. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(piles: list[int]) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `piles`: list[int] of length 4. Each entry is the number of objects remaining in that pile. - Example: `piles = [1, 3, 5, 7]`. # Action / Return Format - Return a move as a string in the format `'pile,take'` (both are integers, comma-separated, no extra text). - `pile` is the 0-based pile index (0-3). - `take` is how many objects to remove from that pile (must be >= 1). - The move is legal iff `1 <= take <= state['piles'][pile]`. - The game ends when all piles are zero. The player who takes the last object loses. - Your goal is to choose an optimal move (perfect play). # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
This is misère Nim, where taking the last object makes you lose. I'm working out the strategy: if all piles have at most 1 object, the player to move wins when the number of non-empty piles is even; otherwise, the standard approach is to play normal Nim by zeroing the xor, but with a special exception—avoid leaving a position where all piles are 1 unless it leaves an odd count of them.

For the case with exactly one pile bigger than 1, I want to leave an odd number of 1-piles for the opponent, adjusting the big pile to 0 or 1 depending on the parity of existing ones. For two or more big piles, computing the xor and reducing one pile to zero it out works safely since another pile stays above 1. If already at a losing xor-zero position, I just make any legal move, like taking one from the largest pile, to keep things going.
